phase1.intro:
Every field and method you've built with me so far has belonged to one specific object. static members break that rule on purpose.

What do you want to look at first?

topics.buttonText: What's the difference between static and instance variables?
dialogue: Watch `staticCount` in the example: every single `Counter` object nudges the SAME shared number, like they're all writing tally marks on one whiteboard bolted to the wall, while `instanceCount` resets fresh for each object, like each one gets their own private notepad.
[[key:instance variables are per-object, static variables are shared across every object of that class]] — that's the whole distinction, and everything else in this lesson follows from it.

stickyNote.definition: Instance variables have a separate copy per object. Static variables have one single copy shared by every object of the class.

topics.buttonText: How do static methods and static blocks behave?
dialogue: [[warn:A static method can't directly touch instance variables]], because a static method isn't attached to any particular object — there's no `this` to reach into. You call it on the class itself, `Counter.displayStatic()`, never needing an object.
A [[term:static block]] — `static { ... }` — runs exactly once, the very first time the blueprint gets loaded, before even `main()` starts.

stickyNote.flavor: 🧱 no this, called on the class, runs once at load
stickyNote.definition: Static methods can't access instance variables (no this). A static block runs once, when the class is first loaded, before main().

topics.buttonText: What makes static final the standard way to write a constant?
dialogue: `static final` together is the standard way to write a real constant — `static final double PI = 3.14159;` — [[key:one shared value, and static final means it can never change]].
The entire `Math` class is built almost entirely out of static methods — that's exactly why you never need a `Math` object to call `Math.sqrt(16)`.

stickyNote.definition: static final double PI = 3.14159; creates one shared, unchangeable value. Math.sqrt() works this way — no object needed.

phase1.openingDialogue: static members belong to the class itself, not any one object — one shared copy, whether it's a variable, method, or block. 🧱

phase2.errorMessage:
Counter.java:8: error: non-static variable instanceValue cannot be referenced from a static context
        instanceValue = 10;  // ERROR!
        ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:A static method has no attached object, so it has no way to reach instanceValue]] — instance variables only exist once an object has actually been created, and a static method can be called with zero objects in existence at all.

[[key:There are really three honest ways to fix this]]: make `instanceValue` static too, if it genuinely should be shared across every object; access it through a specific object reference (`someCounter.instanceValue`) instead of directly; or simply don't try to touch instance state from a static method at all. [[key:The rule to remember is simple]]: a static context can only directly reach other static members.

mcq.question:
Why can't a static method directly access an instance variable?

A) Instance variables are always private
B) A static method isn't tied to any specific object, so there's no instance to read the variable from
C) Static methods run before instance variables are created in memory
D) This restriction doesn't actually exist

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a Student class with:
• Instance fields: name (String), grade (int)
• Static field: schoolName (String) — shared by all students
• Static method: setSchoolName(String name) — sets the school name
• Constructor: sets name and grade
• Method: displayInfo() — prints all info

In main, create 3 students, set school name once, and display all.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: a static block doesn't necessarily run the moment your program starts — it runs the first time that specific class actually gets loaded by the JVM, which in a big program might be well after main() begins, whenever something first references that class.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you share more state~
